text: Under agenda item 5.1, to St. Marie Community Greenhouse Gas Reduction Plan, 2020-2030, Emily Cormier, the Climate Change Coordinator with Future Sault Ste. Marie, is on the call.

speaker: provenzano
text: Welcome to Council, Emily.

speaker: emilycormier
text: Thank you. Happy to be here. Perfect. Thank you. So for those watching at home who don't know, my name is Emily Cormier, and this evening I will be presenting the City of Sault Ste. Marie's Community Greenhouse Gas Reduction Plan, 2020-2030. Before I begin, I just wanted to take a moment to acknowledge some of the stakeholders who've been such an instrumental part for this one and a half year project. This list is by no means complete, but I would like to just extend my thanks to a couple of folks who I'll read now. Thank you to Algoma Steel, the PUC, Garden River First Nation, Algoma Public Health, Clean North, and thank you to the many City of Sault Ste. Marie staff who've been involved in this project. And lastly, I'd like to acknowledge the funder of this project, the Federation of Canadian Municipalities. Next slide, please. Before I dive into an overview of the plan, I just wanted to bring forward a couple of insights regarding climate change. Climate change is something that we hear about a lot. We hear about it in the media, we hear about it in social media, and it truly is the defining issue of our time. We have about 10 years to really limit global warming to one and a half degrees Celsius below pre-industrial levels or face irreversible economic, environmental, and social impacts. There is an opportunity here, however, as you can see for every dollar invested in climate change mitigation, we save three to $5 in recovery costs. Clean innovation is also a fast growing market set to be valued worth $2.5 trillion by 2022. From a reputational standpoint, it is also very opportune. As you can see here, Vancouver's green brand is valued at $31 billion. So as much as this plan addresses the environment, it also addresses the economy. Next slide, please. There are a variety of methodologies that can be used in developing a climate change action plan. The City of Sault Ste. Marie opted to use the Federation of Canadian Municipalities Partners for Climate Protection Program. This program has over 400 members across Canada, and it guides them through a five-step milestone process with the ultimate goal of implementing a climate change action plan. The City of Sault Ste. Marie completed milestone one in February of this year with the completion of the GHG emissions inventory. If approved, this plan will complete milestones two and three and lay the groundwork for milestones four and five of the methodology. Next slide, please. I wanted to take a moment as well to highlight some of the great sustainability efforts that the municipality has been involved in over the years. This diagram highlights a series of plans, initiatives, and programs. Specifically, the Green Committee has been around since 2007. They've done a lot of great work. Also, the corporate GHG emissions inventory was first completed in 2009. And of course, the Energy Conservation and Demand Management Plan, which is mandated by the province. All of these plans do address sustainability in one shape or form, but other than the corporate emissions inventory, they don't address climate change head-on, which really reiterated the need for this project. The City of Sault Ste. Marie has also been working on climate change adaptation work as shown in the climate change risk assessment, which was completed in February of this year. Next slide, please. So diving into the plan here, the community GHG reduction plan was developed using a three-tiered approach. The first phase, as I mentioned, was the community emissions inventory, and this wrapped up in the early part of this year. The second stage was the stakeholder consultations, which wrapped up in the spring. And we used both of these stages, the insights obtained to create the plan itself. The plan is comprised of 60 actions, 14 of which are already in progress, and they include objectives, responsibilities, timelines, and performance measures. Each section of the plan is also furthered by a list of supporting programs, policies, rather, and legislation, as well as funding and financing opportunities. Energy efficiency is at the core of this plan, which aligns very well with the recently completed Sault Ste. Marie third-party service review, which estimates that energy efficiency can reduce energy costs by about $100,000 a year. This was completely bang on for 2020 as energy savings incentives, as well as utility sponsorship, resulted in approximately $106,000. Next slide, please. So just as a refresher here, you can see this is a reminder about what our emissions inventory looked like. Based on 2017 baseline data, the city of Sault Ste. Marie emitted approximately 1.5 million tons of carbon dioxide equivalent. 1% of emissions were from municipal operations, with the majority of emissions coming from fleet and equipment. The remainder of community emissions were the larger portion of the inventory, with the majority coming from the built environment, specifically the use of industrial natural gas. The second highest source of emissions came from on-road transportation, which is very common throughout the rest of the province. Next slide, please. As I mentioned, the second phase of the GHG reduction plan were stakeholder consultations. So this is where we went out in the community and we asked residents and businesses what were some opportunities and challenges they saw with regards to reducing emissions. I'm pleased to say that we really initiated a rather robust approach to our outreach activities, and we reached over 300 participants who were able to provide feedback. Of note here, we had an open house, we consulted with 17 stakeholders one-on-one, we had three surveys that we administered to youth, residents, as well as the city's green committee, and we had four community pop-up consultations pre-COVID where we were able to access insights from folks who may not have been able to attend the open house. Next slide, please. So what did we hear? Some of the benefits that were identified in our consultations were really the need to increase awareness about climate change. So really understanding that the energy that we use every day to heat our homes and to get to and from work and school do produce emissions. They also, emissions also have the opportunity to save money and support local businesses in food production, as well as increase waste diversion. Some of the opportunities that were identified were to increase transit ridership, as well as the adoption of electric vehicles. Energy conservation and retrofits were really identified as a core pillar, as well as increasing and maintaining our green space and urban forest canopy. Some of the barriers identified in the plan were we really have limited resources focused on sustainability here in Sault Ste. Marie, and even though energy efficiency projects are ideal, they can sometimes be a bit difficult to obtain due to high capital costs. We also have fairly limited density in our community at the moment, so we have a very high reliance on personal vehicle use. As far as priorities, energy management in all existing assets and new builds should be key, as well as continuing to consult with local industry to really understand and perhaps partner with them on their planned GHG reduction projects, as well as encouraging green job development and landfill waste diversion. Next slide, please. So the plan itself is broken down into seven key sectors based on emission sources, as well as reduction action opportunities. So the sectors are buildings and energy, looking at the community as well as municipal emissions, transportation and waste, green space, economic development, and municipal leadership. As required under, or as we can voluntarily do under milestone two of the PCP program, the city has opted to create a target for emissions reduction. And the city's goal for GHG reduction is net zero by 2050. The city will take a staged approach to achieve this goal and will focus on a GHG reduction target of 10% corporate and 5% community between 2020 and 2030, with an increasing scale of reduction target between 2030 and 2050. Next slide, please. So we just wanted to highlight that in addition to the seven sectors identified in the plan, there were a series of guiding principles that align with emissions mitigation action that were extrapolated from the community consultations. And these really highlight a series of reoccurring opportunities that really can integrate into our climate change action across multiple sectors. So as you can see here, climate action can help with affordability by reducing energy costs and improving for access to economical housing, accountability, ensuring that we have a sustainable future for our next generations, increasing education and awareness, as well as community pride by increasing community wellbeing, as well as economic development through clean technology business development and even ecotourism. We'll protect our environment and habitat by protecting species at risk and our forest from climate impacts and also improve community health and access to food security. Next slide, please. So, as I said, this plan has 60 actions and they're rather robust, but you highlight the priorities, they can really be divided into two key sectors. So the first pillar really is climate change capacity. And we've got some great progress on this with the establishment of the new Environmental Sustainability Committee. So next steps would include appointing this committee and holding their first meeting. Also, it would be a good idea to create a climate information webpage on city website, sort of as a one-stop shop for climate information for the community, continue exploring budgeting and funding requirements in particular for the year one priorities, as well as undertaking a youth-led environmental sustainability community project and governance and leadership. So really ensuring that city policies and programs align with supporting the GHG reduction plan. This plan cannot be implemented by focusing on just one department. It truly is a operation-wide endeavor. The second pillar of priorities, of course, is GHG emissions reduction. So really focusing here on prioritizing energy efficiency retrofits, as well as zero emission fleet opportunities. A priority will also be to summarize departmental initiatives and actions by each city department. Increasing tree planting and conducting an urban tree canopy study to also understand our carbon offset potential should also be a priority, as well as exploring the possibility of developing a community retrofit program and streamlining the city's mandatory energy reporting process. Next slide, please. The plan identifies a series of internal and external financing and funding opportunities. From an internal standpoint, the city can access federal gas tax funding that can be allocated to infrastructure projects, community energy systems, public transit, studies and training, as well as waste reduction. The city also recently allocated $50,000 from the Community Development Fund for green initiatives that nonprofits and city departments can apply to for projects that reduce emissions, improve energy efficiency, and improve upon water quality. Other ideas could include developing a corporate internal revolving energy fund, which would use savings from energy retrofits, for example, and use those savings to be invested into other green initiatives. Another opportunity would be to look at developing a local improvement charge for energy efficiency projects. This was recently updated to the Ontario Municipal Act in 2012, it basically is a low interest retrofit loan tied to a residential property. From an external standpoint, it's exciting to see as we move forward into the COVID-19 recovery, a lot of the stimulus is really geared towards green growth. $10 billion, for example, has been earmarked for zero emission buses, two and a half billion for clean power, as well as energy efficient building retrofits. Not included in this plan was the recently updated Canadian environmental plan, a healthy environment and healthy economy, which was launched last Friday, which also earmarks about $3 billion towards tree planting. The COVID-19 resiliency funding has funding available for energy efficiency retrofits, active transportation, as well as tree planting, and the Enbridge and IESO conservation programs, which have been around for a while are still around and are a great opportunity to finance energy efficiency retrofits. The Federation of Canadian Municipalities Green Municipal Fund funds municipal projects that are green for pilots, studies, as well as capital projects. And since their inception, they have spent about $862 million on municipal green projects. And last but not least, the Federation of Canadian Municipalities has launched a community efficiency financing program, which allows municipalities to develop a community retrofit program using the local improvement charge model. I'd also like to highlight that the city should also consider adding a criteria to capital and operating budget requests that would review requests as well as based on their impact to environmental sustainability. Next slide, please. So as part of the implementation process, a variety of scenarios were reviewed. As you can see here, some of their benefits and limitations are identified. However, it is recommended that the city assign responsibility to the Environmental Sustainability Committee, which is already in progress, to review and oversee the implementation of the plan. It's also recommended that a staff resource be assigned or established to further create a culture of sustainability within the organization. Next slide, please. So as far as next steps go, it's important to review the plan and review next year's projects aimed at reducing corporate and community energy use and emissions. In the plan, there is a section focused on the top 10 priorities for year one. Some of these projects are already underway and they'll really lay the foundation for more complex projects in the future. We'll get the Environmental Sustainability to hold their first committee meeting to really talk about their strategies and priorities for the first year and continue looking for budget and funding requirements for those year one priorities. As I mentioned, this is a five milestone framework that the city has used. So upon approval of this plan, the next two stages will be implementation and monitoring progress and reporting results. It is recommended to review the results fairly regularly to make sure that we're staying on top of our tasks. And I'd like to conclude my presentation this evening by saying that this plan should be viewed as a living document. As I mentioned, the Canadian Climate Change Plan was recently updated last Friday. This is a very fast moving sector with a lot of stimulus funding and new technology developments happening fairly regularly. So it's important that this plan be updated and adapted regularly to acknowledge changing technology, funding and legislative initiatives. Next slide, please. Thank you so much for your attention. I'm open for questions.

speaker: provenzano
text: Thank you, Councilor Shoemaker. Any other matters on consent, Council? Seeing none, we've accepted 15, so we can vote on the consent agenda, Madam Clerk. All in favor? Carried. That brings us to 6.15. And maybe, Madam Clerk, I'll start with whomever, was it Councilor Shoemaker or Councilor Christian who offered the amendment? Councilor Shoemaker, so we'll start with you. We'll start with you, Councilor Shoemaker, since you had offered the amendment.

speaker: councillorshoema
text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Mayor. Just for some background on this, I, myself and Councilor Grandinetti had brought the motion looking to level the playing field for local improvement charges across various classes of roads a number of years ago, because at present, only class A roads are charged local improvements when they are constructed or reconstructed. An excellent report came back from Mr. Elliott, and the city clerk, I understand, was also integral in the drafting of this, except that the result of the report would have ended up with the city having less revenue in future years from local improvement charges than we do at present. So the amendment, Councilor Christian and I discussed or over the weekend and put forward is to make the changes revenue neutral to the city so that we are not bringing in any more money from the changes in the local improvement charges, but so that we are not bringing in any less either. The only other comment that I would, or the only other matter I would address is that this really does make the system a lot fairer because as I mentioned, historically only class A roads were being charged for construction or reconstruction. This will level the playing field across class B and class C roads. And this is, I would say an excellent example of our municipality using a revenue tool at its disposal that other municipalities don't. So we often discuss that issue at Council. And this is one example where we are doing something that other municipalities aren't and have been for a long time. So I think it's good to continue the process of applying local improvement charges as it's come to be almost not expected, but accepted by residents.

speaker: provenzano
text: Okay, Councilor Christian, did you, so just so we're clear, everybody has the recommendation in front of them. Madam Clerk, is the amendment to the motion in front of us, the recommendation in front of us, is that also on East Drive? Do all the Councilors have that amendment?

speaker: racheltyczinksi
text: It is on East Drive. If you'd like, I'll read the motion as it first appeared and then I'll read the amending motion.

speaker: provenzano
text: Yeah, please do. So everybody's working for the same playbook.

speaker: racheltyczinksi
text: So this is the original motion. And I just would add that the amendment is to change item C and to add a word to item F. The original motion was moved by Councilor Shoemaker and Hollingsworth, resolved as a report of the Director of Engineering and City Clerk dated December 14, 2020, regarding local improvement policy be received and that the existing procedure be amended beginning with the 2021 Capital Transportation Program to A, discontinue charging local improvements for reconstruction of sanitary sewage infrastructure, B, continue charging local improvements for construction of new sanitary infrastructure, C, and this will be amended, continue to charge local improvements for new Class A roads and one half new construction rates for reconstruction, D, begin charging local improvements for new Class B and C roads and one half new construction rates for reconstruction, E, upon a sufficient petition of benefiting property owners, charge local improvements for new Class A, B, or C construction, and F, implement local improvement charges as recommended with an annual estimated CPI increase. And that the amendment by Councilor Shoemaker and Christian is resolved that the main motion be amended by replacing the words in existing paragraph C with the following, continue to charge local improvements for new Class A roads at a rate that equals the historic local improvement and sanitary rate combined and one half the new construction rates for reconstruction. And by adding the word new between the words implement and improvement in paragraph F so that it reads implement new local improvement charges as recommended with the annual CPI increase.

speaker: provenzano
text: Okay, Council, do you have any questions about those amendments? So we're just dealing with the amendment right now. Do you have any questions about the amendment? Councilor Dufour.

speaker: dufour
text: Yeah, I'm just a little bit, I guess my question is, if we're recovering the cost of sanitary sewer reconstruction through the reserve, why would we still need to collect it? Like wouldn't the revenue that we're losing just be covered by a subtraction from the sanitary reserve?

speaker: provenzano
text: So, yeah, I understand the question. I'm going to go to the city engineer here. Don, did you understand the question?

speaker: donelliott
text: Yes, I did Mr. Mayor to Councilor Dufour. What's happened in the past is the revenue that was collected for sanitary sewer under the local improvement wasn't put over to the sewer surcharge. So it is revenue that affects the levy, it affects the capital budget. So I believe the amendment is intends to have this be a revenue neutral situation. So that's why the sanitary rate would be added in and blended into the new rate.

speaker: dufour
text: Okay, would it be a little clearer if the new rate was just still simply like didn't have any reference to the sanitary rate?

speaker: donelliott

speaker: dufour
text: Okay, it will just be equal to that previous amount that was misalloc, I don't want to say misallocated, but perhaps mislabeled as to its use?

speaker: donelliott

speaker: dufour
text: Okay, and it will be comprised of the amount that is currently in the levy for that collection?

speaker: donelliott
text: That's correct.
